notes.meaning: Rachel finally became pregnant and gave birth to a baby boy. In that culture, childlessness was viewed as a heavy public disgrace, so she praised God for taking away her shame. God heard her long prayers and showed her mercy in his own time.

Rachel named the baby Joseph, a name connected with Hebrew words meaning to take away and to add. She openly declared her faith that the Lord would add another son to her family. God later fulfilled that hope when Benjamin was born.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest the two wordplays for Joseph's name and the shift from God to the Lord come from two separate ancient written sources that were joined together.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some traditional Catholic commentators point out that while Rachel prayed for another son, receiving that blessing later cost her own life during childbirth.

notes.meaning: After Joseph was born, Jacob asked Laban for permission to return to his homeland. Jacob had now completed his full fourteen years of agreed service for his two wives. Even though he had no wealth of his own yet, he trusted God's promise to bring him back to Canaan.

Jacob asked Laban to release his wives and children so they could begin their journey. He had earned them through years of exhausting, honest labor, and Laban knew how hard he had worked. Jacob did not demand any extra gifts, but simply asked for what was rightfully his.

Laban begged Jacob to stay because he realized that the Lord had blessed his estate because of Jacob. Whether Laban learned this through close observation or through fortune-telling rituals, he recognized the true source of his wealth. God often grants outward success even to selfish people for the sake of his servants who dwell among them.

Laban urged Jacob to name his own wage, promising to pay whatever was asked. Laban made a show of great generosity, but his real aim was to keep Jacob managing his herds. He suspected that Jacob was humble and would ask for far less than his hard work was truly worth.

Jacob reminded Laban how faithfully he had tended the flocks for many years. Under Jacob's constant care, Laban's livestock had remained healthy and multiplied rapidly. Jacob spoke plainly so Laban would recognize that he deserved fair compensation.

Jacob pointed out that Laban had owned very little before Jacob arrived, but now owned great wealth. The Lord had multiplied the herds wherever Jacob set foot to work. Now that Jacob had a large family, he rightly needed to provide for his own household.

When Laban asked what he should pay, Jacob replied that he did not want regular fixed wages. Instead, he proposed an unusual agreement that would leave his future earnings entirely in God's hands. If Laban agreed to this single condition, Jacob would gladly continue shepherding the flocks.

Jacob offered to go through the flocks that day and separate out every spotted, speckled, or dark animal. Sheep in that region were almost always solid white, and goats were usually solid black or brown, making spotted animals quite rare. Jacob agreed that only future young born with these uncommon markings would count as his pay.

Jacob explained that his honesty would be easy to prove whenever Laban inspected the animals. If any solid-colored goat or lamb was ever found in Jacob's pens, it would count as stolen. Jacob trusted the Lord to reward his integrity openly in the sight of his master.

Laban quickly agreed to the terms because the offer seemed entirely in his own favor. He assumed that solid-colored parents would naturally produce solid-colored offspring, leaving Jacob with almost nothing. Laban was pleased to keep Jacob's skilled service for next to no cost.

Laban took no chances and immediately removed all the spotted goats and dark lambs himself that very day. He placed those animals into the care of his own sons so Jacob could not claim them. This ensured that Jacob started his new agreement tending only solid-colored animals.

Laban put a three-day journey between his sons' spotted herds and the rest of the flocks Jacob tended. He created this distance so the two groups could not accidentally mix or breed together. Jacob was left behind to care for Laban's remaining solid-colored animals.
Jacob cut fresh, moist branches from poplar, almond, and plane trees. He peeled away stripes of the dark bark to expose the bright white inner wood. This gave the rods a patterned, spotted look.

Jacob set the striped branches in the watering troughs where the animals gathered to drink. When the flocks came to drink, they were also in heat and would mate near the troughs. The patterned sticks were placed directly in front of the animals as they bred.

The animals mated in front of the peeled branches and gave birth to young that were streaked, speckled, and spotted. Shepherds in the ancient world believed that visual sights during breeding shaped the markings of the offspring. God worked through these events to bless Jacob and keep his promises.

Jacob set the spotted young apart from the main flock. He then turned Laban's solid-colored animals so they faced toward the striped and dark ones during feeding. He kept his own spotted flocks separate so they would not mix with Laban's stock.

Jacob displayed the peeled branches only when the stronger and healthier animals were ready to breed. This ensured that the sturdiest lambs and kids would be born with spots and belong to his own flock. Jacob applied his deep knowledge of sheep breeding throughout the season.

Whenever the weaker animals bred, Jacob kept the peeled branches out of the troughs. As a result, the weaker offspring were born solid-colored and went to Laban, while the stronger ones went to Jacob. In this way, Jacob steadily built up a healthy, high-quality flock.

Jacob grew exceedingly wealthy in a very short time. He acquired vast herds of livestock, along with male and female servants, camels, and donkeys. God stepped in to bless Jacob's hard labor and restored the wages that Laban had tried to deny him.
